# Decentralized CAR-T manufacturing: highlighting regulatory pathways in the United States and abroad 

Nirav N. Shah,

Kaitlin Annunzio,

Abstract

Regulators worldwide are increasingly evaluating how decentralized and point-of-care (POC) manufacturing models can be integrated into existing frameworks for cell and gene therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies. These models challenge traditional centralized production by distributing manufacturing across several clinical or academic sites, requiring new approaches to ensure product consistency, traceability, and good manufacturing practice (GMP) compliance. Across jurisdictions, regulators are converging on several common themes. First, decentralization must operate under a unified quality management system with clearly defined oversight, typically anchored by a central “control” or coordinating site responsible for governance, batch oversight, and harmonized procedures. Second, comparability across sites is critical, necessitating standardized processes, validated technologies, and robust data systems to support real-time quality monitoring. Third, regulators emphasize that decentralized models do not reduce GMP requirements; rather, they require additional structures to ensure alignment across distributed facilities. Many authorities are exploring mechanisms to clarify roles and responsibilities within POC networks, including oversight; documentation standards; and expectations for training, inspection, and data integrity. Some regulators are also assessing how existing pathways, such as hospital exemptions, accelerated approval mechanisms, or special designations, could support early clinical use while maintaining rigorous safety and quality controls. In parallel, discussion papers, stakeholder consultations, and emerging guidance reflect a shared interest in addressing technological advances such as automated, closed-system manufacturing. In this article, we review and discuss work being done in this regard across Europe, Canada, and the United States.

## Introduction

Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed the therapeutic landscape for relapsed or refractory (R/R) hematologic malignancies and holds increasing promise for solid tumors and autoimmune diseases. By genetically reprogramming a patient’s own T cells to recognize and eliminate malignant cells, CAR-T therapies have demonstrated durable responses in populations with otherwise limited options. 1, 2 Despite this clinical success, data from the United States and Europe suggest that only 20% to 30% of the clinically eligible patients receive CAR-T therapy, reflecting a complex set of access constraints including geographic and logistical limitations, socioeconomic and racial inequities, health system capacity, and funding and reimbursement barriers. 3-5 A contributor to these access constraints is the current model of CAR-T manufacturing, which remains highly centralized and resource intensive. A limited number of qualified facilities worldwide can produce these products under good manufacturing practice (GMP) conditions, resulting in high production costs and restricted accessibility. 6 Clinical trial and real-world data from US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved CAR-T therapies in the United States show that disease progression or death during manufacturing is the leading reason patients who undergo leukapheresis do not reach CAR-T infusion, underscoring the clinical importance of minimizing vein-to-vein time. 1, 7-9 

These challenges have catalyzed growing interest in point-of-care (POC) manufacturing, an emerging paradigm designed to decentralize cell therapy production and bring manufacturing capability closer to the site of care. This approach offers strategies for reducing vein-to-vein time by manufacturing locally using closed systems, expanding geographic reach to improve equity of access, lowering costs and logistical barriers associated with long-distance shipping and commercial supply chains, and supporting innovation and adaptability. 10-12 

### Defining decentralized manufacturing

There is a spectrum of decentralized models of manufacturing for cell and gene therapies. At its core, it refers to the local or regional manufacture of cellular immunotherapies such as CAR-Ts, using automated or semiautomated closed-system technologies that allow production within hospital-adjacent or institutional facilities. In 2022, the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) in the United States provided definitions for the various ways to decentralize manufacturing. 13 The distributed manufacturing model refers to the manufacturing across large-scale centers, with centralized quality oversight and coordination. In this model, individual centers maintain partial autonomy, each with its own quality management system, but the regulatory interface remains with the centralized overseeing quality program. The POC manufacturing model specifically refers to manufacturing done directly at the hospital or clinic within which the patient is treated, on-site and on demand. Within these decentralized models of manufacturing, there are a multitude of manufacturing aspects that can be centralized or decentralized. With CAR-T therapies, the components required for manufacturing include plasmids, retrovirus, and T cells, followed by quality control assays for product release. Each of these components can be centralized or decentralized. Most commonly, plasmid and virus have been centrally manufactured, whereas the decentralized component has traditionally been T-cell manufacturing. Quality control assays can be centralized, in which product samples are shipped to one site for release vs being done locally at the T-cell manufacturing site. Nonetheless, all these approaches contrast with traditional centralized models, in which patient material is transported to a remote facility, and the final product is shipped back to the clinical center.

### Operationalizing decentralized manufacturing

Decentralized or POC manufacturing has been conventionally supported by advances in closed and automated cell processing systems, which integrate multiple steps of CAR-T production, comprising cell selection, activation, transduction, expansion, and harvest, within a single, enclosed environment. Fully automated systems minimize manual manipulation and contamination risk, whereas modular platforms allow independent optimization of each process step. Automation further enhances traceability and regulatory documentation, enabling harmonized operating procedures across distributed networks. 14 Establishing decentralized networks requires robust technology transfer and onboarding processes, including site qualification, gap assessments, comparability studies, and audits, long before the product can reach clinical trial with multiple manufacturing sites. 15 For example, each site must demonstrate the ability to meet predefined release criteria and certificate-of-analysis standards to ensure product equivalence. Close collaboration between clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory teams is essential to achieve and maintain standardization across locations.

### Centralized vs decentralized manufacturing

Centralized manufacturing offers economies of scale and consolidated expertise but introduces long transport timelines and system vulnerabilities because of single-site dependency. It also provides CAR-T access to centers that want to deliver cell and gene therapies but lack the manufacturing infrastructure or skill set to manufacture onsite. However, extended logistics can delay treatment, increase manufacturing failure risk, and limit patient access, particularly in geographically large regions. In contrast, decentralized or POC manufacturing mitigates these challenges by reducing transport complexity and enabling local, patient-specific production. It shortens vein-to-vein timelines and can allow real-time responsiveness to clinical demand. 16 Decentralized approaches provide the operational flexibility to implement rapid process refinements that optimize product attributes during initial clinical trials. 17 Furthermore, for CAR-T therapies targeting rare diseases that are unlikely to have commercial interest, decentralized manufacturing can support treatment access for small patient populations. 18 

The downside is that decentralization also entails duplication of infrastructure, increased regulatory oversight across multiple facilities, and the challenge of retaining multiple quality systems in distributed settings. Maintaining cross-site equivalence requires harmonized protocols, standardized training, digital batch records, and cross-validation studies. Decentralized models must also address intellectual property, sponsor oversight, and liability management, all of which become more complex when production responsibility is shared across multiple institutions. 19 These challenges mean that upfront investment in infrastructure, automation, and workforce development is needed to launch decentralized manufacturing models. Modeling studies indicate that cost-efficiency improves markedly with scale for these models, with higher production volumes reducing per-product costs. 20 As automation matures, potentially with the integration of artificial intelligence, and regulatory frameworks evolve, these models may ultimately enhance the affordability and accessibility of CAR-T therapy.

Although there are benefits to both centralized and decentralized manufacturing, their place in the pipeline of cell therapies may differ. The optimal manufacturing model for CAR-T therapies may depend on the novelty of the target and the clinical indication being addressed. Early clinical development of novel CAR constructs is often performed using centralized manufacturing platforms that facilitate tight process control and product characterization. As clinical and manufacturing experience with a given construct accumulates, distributed manufacturing models may become increasingly attractive to improve scalability and reduce vein-to-vein time. 21 Similarly, when established CAR platforms are applied to new indications, such as autoimmune diseases, previous manufacturing experience may enable more rapid adoption of distributed models while maintaining product quality and safety, although the appropriate manufacturing strategy may depend on factors including patient population size, treatment urgency, and the required scale of production. 22 Here, we review, through global examples, how regulatory authorities are considering decentralized or POC manufacturing for cell and gene therapy approvals, navigating through different regulatory jurisdictions.

## Europe

### EU regulatory framework for decentralized manufacturing

In the European Union (EU), the manufacture of advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs), including CAR-T therapies, is regulated under the established GMP framework Directive 2001/83/European Community (EC) 23 and Commission Directive EU 2017/1572. 24 The EU introduced a dedicated regulatory framework for ATMPs in response to the rapid scientific and technological evolution of cell and gene-based therapies, which challenge traditional, centralized manufacturing models (provided in EudraLex, volume 4). 25 The dedicated ATMP framework was established to ensure that innovative therapies could be developed and deployed safely across member states while maintaining a harmonized regulatory environment.
